title: ANZ wants to change the way companies shift money overseas
full_text:
ANZ will create a new form of deposit later this year to allow large companies to move funds across borders instantly, the latest step by an Australian lender towards adopting new forms of digital money emerging across the globe.
ANZ is the only Australian bank among 17 major international players ready to issue a new digital form of bank deposit, known as a “tokenised deposit”, on its network, according to Swift – a secure messaging service banks use to communicate about cross-border transactions.
ANZ says it is ahead of rival banks developing new forms of cross-border payments. Paul Rovere
The new form of deposit will let ANZ and other banks in the network instantly move money between corporate accounts used to fund subsidiaries or pay suppliers. Swift’s blockchain technology will allow funds to be received in real-time – even on a weekend – removing delays in cross-border clearing which frustrate global companies.
Australia’s big banks are also making early steps towards another emerging form of private digital money, known as stablecoin. This is also a digital token representing money that moves instantly on a blockchain system. But, unlike a tokenised deposit, the funds backing stablecoins are held in financial reserves controlled by the issuer.
ANZ and its rivals, Commonwealth Bank, National Australia Bank and Westpac, have joined a global stablecoin consortium known as Open USD, the company operating it, Open Standard, said last month.
The initiative is backed by payments giants Visa, Mastercard, Stripe and more than 140 other companies, including Google and many global banks. It will seek to compete with another popular stablecoin known as USD Coin issued by the US technology company Circle.
Visa said this month it has created a new stablecoin platform that will use Open USD. Like Swift, its initial customers will also be companies seeking to move money between jurisdictions with more speed.
Open USD says its reserves will be maintained at major financial institutions, in compliance with US regulatory requirements, and banks using it would pay no fees to “mint” or “redeem” the stablecoin. Visa said its stablecoin platform would facilitate the movement of Open USD funds in an environment banks already trust.
The rapid developments come as the United States has moved to legitimise stablecoins this year under new regulation backed by President Donald Trump.
In Australia, the House of Representatives economics committee, in a report published in late June, called for Treasury to establish a framework “for the enablement of stablecoins as an alternate payment rail within the Australian payments system as a matter of urgency”.
The major banks’ participation in Open USD and ANZ’s interest in the Swift project come just two months after the Reserve Bank of Australia reported on Project Acacia. This explored use cases for stablecoins and tokenised bank deposits and the guardrails needed to support their safe rollout.
The RBA and major commercial banks have created the “Deposit Token Working Group” to develop ways to support the interoperability of deposit tokens issued by different Australian banks.
US and UK banks are moving more aggressively. Last month, large US banks formed a new company, called the Clearing House, which plans to launch a tokenised deposit network next year, according to a report in The Wall Street Journal.
“Once this becomes mainstream, [company] treasuries, if they choose, can conquer the time zone problem of a global business.”
Nigel Dobson, ANZ
Analysts say Australian lenders may be behind the eight-ball on a global movement set to reshape the infrastructure of money over the next two years.
“The Australian banks seem to be lagging global developments in blockchain, stablecoins and AI. It’s not part of the major bank narrative. Why? It’s clearly a threat to profitability,” said Matt Wilson, an analyst at Jarden.
“We see this new technology as a step change in financial infrastructure that will challenge the inertia rents embedded in the major bank system.”
For company treasurers, faster settlement using tokenised money promises to improve working capital management, reduce the need for pre-funding accounts, and create greater certainty over cash flows. Unlike stablecoins, interest can be paid on tokenised deposits, as they are moved around the world.
“The problem this solves is 24/7 liquidity for treasury management,” says Nigel Dobson, banking services portfolio lead at ANZ.
“The biggest complaint from corporate treasurers is the ‘disappearance’ of their money over a weekend. This creates just-in-time funding, which allows the customer to have a 24/7 liquidity experience, while the banks manage settlement between themselves.
“Once that becomes mainstream, these treasuries, if they choose, can conquer the time zone problem of a global business.”
For banks and regulators, tokenised deposits are more attractive than stablecoins because the money stays inside the banking system, allowing lenders to operate under existing regulatory frameworks.
Global investment bank JPMorgan has created its own system for moving tokenised deposits known as Kinexys Blockchain Deposit Accounts. Australian dollar transactions are now available on the platform, which is also being used to automate treasury and liquidity management across markets.
“The near-term value proposition of using tokenised deposits for corporate treasury is clear: faster movement of value, better liquidity visibility across entities, and fewer cut-off constraints across time zones,” said Max Neukirchen, global co-head of payments at JPMorgan.
UK banks are also making moves in the space. Like the big US banks, Barclays, HSBC, Lloyds and other lenders have formed the “Great British Tokenised Deposit initiative” to build the country’s first tokenised deposit payments platform.
But Britain also recognises different forms of tokenised money will co-exist in the future. The country’s ’Wholesale Digital Markets Champion”, Christopher Woolard, called for British pound-denominated stablecoins to be issued at scale.
“Establishing a robust and domestic stablecoin ecosystem will be critical to strengthen the UK’s competitiveness and operational resilience, safeguarding its strategic position in an increasingly complex geopolitical environment,” Woolard said in a report sent to the UK Chancellor this month.
Australia’s stablecoin licensing reforms passed the federal Parliament in April.
